meta.title: The path
meta.why: One lesson at a time, in order, with one button. No choosing what to study and no menus to get lost in. Pinyin first, because you cannot learn a word whose sound you cannot hear or say. Then common words, then phrases, with reading mixed in once the sounds are solid.

units.title: Pinyin — reading the sounds
units.goal: Look at any pinyin syllable and know exactly how it sounds.

units.title: Your first words
units.goal: Twenty words you will use in every conversation.

units.title: What the characters mean
units.goal: See a character and know what it means and which parts it is built from.

units.title: Your first sentences
units.goal: Say and understand real sentences built from those words.

steps.title: Chinese has no alphabet
steps.body: This trips up everyone. There is no A-B-C. Instead there are two completely separate systems, and you only need the first one to speak.

steps.title: 1. Pinyin — the sounds
steps.body: Every Chinese syllable written in Latin letters. This is what you will learn first, and it is the closest thing to an alphabet. It is also a trap: the letters do NOT say what an English speaker expects.

steps.title: 2. Characters — the writing
steps.body: Not letters at all — each character is a whole meaning. You do not need them to speak, so they stay optional. But you will see them everywhere, so every new word shows what its characters mean, and a short unit right after your first words shows how they are built.

steps.title: Every syllable has three parts
steps.body: An initial (the starting consonant), a final (the rest), and a tone (the pitch). That is the whole system — about 400 possible syllables, and you are about to learn all the pieces.

steps.question: Which one do you need in order to SPEAK Chinese?

options.label: Pinyin — the sounds
options.why: Right. Speaking is sound. Characters are a reading skill you can add later, or never.

options.label: Characters
options.why: Not yet. Characters are for reading and writing. You can hold a conversation without knowing a single one.

steps.title: That is lesson one
steps.body: Next: the one thing that makes Chinese genuinely different from English — tones. Take it slowly; this is the part worth getting right.

steps.title: In English, pitch carries mood
steps.body: "Really." and "Really?" are the same word. Your voice going up only signals a question — it does not make it a different word.

steps.title: In Chinese, pitch IS the word
steps.body: The syllable "ma" said at four different pitches is four unrelated words: mother, hemp, horse, to scold. Get the pitch wrong and you have said something else entirely.

steps.title: Listen to the four shapes
steps.body: These are pure tones, not speech — just the pitch shape, so nothing can get in the way. Play each one. You are listening for the SHAPE, not the sound.

steps.title: Tone 1 — high and flat
steps.body: Hold one high note, steady, like singing. It does not move. Think of a doctor saying "say ahhh".

steps.title: Tone 2 — rising
steps.body: Starts mid, goes up. Exactly like the English "huh?" when you did not catch something.

steps.title: Tone 3 — low
steps.body: The textbook says it dips down then rises. In real speech it mostly just stays LOW. Think of a disappointed "hmm...". Going low is what matters.

steps.title: Tone 4 — falling
steps.body: Starts high, drops hard and fast. Like a sharp "No!" or "Stop!". It is short and it is angry-sounding.

steps.question: Which tone shape did you hear?
Which tone shape did you hear?

steps.title: Good
steps.body: You do not need to produce these yet. Recognising them comes first — the mouth follows the ear, never the other way round.

steps.title: Just listening today
steps.body: Eight questions. Guessing is completely fine — this is ear training, and it works even while it still feels random. That feeling goes away.

steps.title: That is the hardest part of Chinese
steps.body: Genuinely. Everything after this is vocabulary and practice. Come back to this lesson any time it feels shaky.

steps.title: This is the pair everyone confuses
steps.body: Tone 2 rises. Tone 3 goes low. Both can end up sounding "not flat", which is why beginners mix them. The difference is where they START.

steps.title: Hear them back to back
steps.body: Tone 2 starts in the middle and climbs. Tone 3 drops to the bottom first. Play them until the difference is obvious.

steps.title: The trick
steps.body: Do not listen for the rise. Listen for the LOW. If the voice dips to the bottom of its range, it is tone 3. If it sets off upward from the middle, it is tone 2.

steps.title: One rule you will need constantly
steps.body: When two tone-3 syllables meet, the FIRST becomes tone 2. 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo. This happens everywhere, and doing it makes you sound dramatically more natural.

lessons.title: The letters that lie: q, x, j

steps.title: Now the letters themselves
steps.body: Pinyin uses Latin letters for sounds English does not have. Three of them cause more confusion than everything else combined.

steps.title: q is NOT "kw"
steps.body: Like the ch in "cheap". 去 qù is said roughly "chü" — never "koo". This one word appears constantly, so it is worth fixing now.

steps.title: x is NOT "ks" or "z"
steps.body: Like the sh in "sheep", but lighter and further forward. 谢谢 xièxie is "shyeh-shyeh" — this is how you say thank you, so you will use it every day.

steps.title: j is the easy one
steps.body: Like the j in "jeep". All three — j, q, x — are made with the tongue flat and the lips spread as if smiling. Smile and they come out right.

options.label: "chü"
options.why: Correct. q is always a ch sound.

options.label: "koo"
options.why: That is the English reflex, and it is the single most common pinyin mistake. q is ch.

options.label: "kwoo"
options.why: No — q is never a k or kw sound in pinyin. It is ch.

steps.question: How does 谢谢 xièxie start?

options.label: "sh" as in sheep
options.why: Right. x is a light sh.

options.label: "ks" as in box
options.why: No. Pinyin x is never ks — it is a light sh.

options.label: "z" as in zoo
options.why: No. That is the Spanish/Portuguese habit. Pinyin x is sh.

lessons.title: The letters that lie: c, z, and curled tongues

steps.title: c is "ts"
steps.body: Like the ts at the end of "cats". Never a k, never an s. 从 cóng is "tsong".

steps.title: z is "ds"
steps.body: Like the ds at the end of "kids" — not an English z. 在 zài is "dsigh".

steps.title: zh, ch, sh — tongue curled back
steps.body: Same as j, q, x but with the tongue curled up and back instead of flat. zh ≈ j in "jar", ch ≈ ch in "char", sh ≈ sh in "shine". Flat versus curled is the whole distinction.

steps.title: The silent i
steps.body: After zi ci si zhi chi shi ri, the letter i is NOT "ee". It is just a buzz — hold the consonant and add voice. Saying "shee" for 是 shì is one of the loudest beginner giveaways.

options.label: "shrr" — a buzz, no ee
options.why: Correct. The i after sh is a buzz, not a vowel.

options.label: "shee"
options.why: This is the common mistake. After sh, the i is not "ee" — it is a held buzz.

options.label: ts, as in cats
options.why: Right.

options.label: k, as in cat
options.why: No — pinyin c is never a k sound.

options.label: s, as in city
options.why: Close but no: it needs the t in front. ts.

steps.title: The five basic vowels
steps.body: a = "ah". o = "aw". i = "ee". u = "oo". And e on its own = "uh", as in "the" — NOT "eh". 喝 hē is "huh", not "hay".

steps.title: The sixth vowel: ü
steps.body: English does not have it. Say "ee" — then, without moving your tongue at all, round your lips into a whistle. That is ü. 女 nǚ (woman) uses it.

steps.title: ü hides after j, q, x and y
steps.body: After those letters the two dots get dropped, but the sound stays ü. So ju qu xu yu are really jü qü xü yü. This is why 去 is "chü" and not "choo".

steps.question: In 去 qù, what is the vowel really?

options.label: ü — the dots are just dropped after q
options.why: Exactly. After j, q, x, y the dots vanish but the sound does not.

options.label: u as in "soon"
options.why: It looks that way, but no. After q the u is always ü.

steps.title: Where the dots stay
steps.body: Only after n and l are the dots written, because there both sounds genuinely exist: 女 nǚ (woman) and 努 nǔ (to strive) are different words.

steps.title: -ian is "yen"
steps.body: Despite the spelling it does not rhyme with "ahn". 天 tiān (sky) is "tyen". 钱 qián (money) is "chyen".

steps.title: iu, ui and un hide a vowel
steps.body: iu is really i-o-u, so 六 liù is "lyoh". ui is really u-e-i, so 对 duì is "dway". un is really u-e-n. The missing vowel always sits in the middle.

steps.title: b d g are not really b d g
steps.body: Mandarin does not contrast voiced and voiceless. It contrasts puff of air. b d g have NO puff; p t k have a big one. Hold your hand in front of your mouth: b should not move it, p should.

options.label: "tyen"
options.why: Right — -ian rhymes with English "yen".

options.label: "tyahn"
options.why: The spelling suggests it, but no. -ian is "yen".

steps.title: You can now read pinyin
steps.body: That is the whole sound system. From here on, every new word comes with pinyin you can actually decode — which is exactly why we did this first. Now let's use it on real words.

steps.title: Your first word
steps.body: Literally "you good". Two syllables, both written tone 3 — which means the sandhi rule from lesson 4 applies: it is actually said ní hǎo.

steps.note: The person radical 亻 on the left tells you this word is about a person.
A woman 女 next to a child 子 — the old image of 'good'.

steps.question: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo. How is it actually said?

options.label: ní hǎo — the first tone 3 becomes tone 2
options.why: Correct. Two tone 3s in a row: the first changes. This happens every time.

options.label: nǐ hǎo — both stay low
options.why: That is what is written, but not what is said. Two tone 3s never sit side by side in speech.

steps.title: That is a real Chinese word
steps.body: You can now greet someone. Next: the words for I, you and he.

lessons.title: 我 你 他 — I, you, he

steps.title: Three pronouns, no changes
steps.body: Good news: Chinese pronouns never change form. No I/me/my/mine. 我 is all four.

steps.note: A hand 手 holding a weapon 戈 — the one defending myself.
Person 亻 + 也. Swap 亻 for 女 and you get 她 — she. Same sound exactly.

steps.title: Making them plural
steps.body: Add 们 men. 我们 = we. 你们 = you (plural). 他们 = they. One rule, no exceptions.

options.label: we / us
options.why: Right — 我 (I) + 们 (plural).

options.label: they
options.why: That is 他们. 我们 starts with 我, which is 'I'.

lessons.title: 是 and 不 — is, and not

steps.title: One word for am, is and are
steps.body: 是 never changes. 我是 = I am. 你是 = you are. 他是 = he is. No conjugation anywhere in Chinese.

steps.note: Put it directly in front of the verb: 我不是 = I am not.

steps.title: 不 changes its own tone
steps.body: 不 is tone 4, but when the next word is ALSO tone 4 it flips to tone 2. So 不是 is said bú shì. Same idea as the tone 3 rule — Chinese avoids stacking identical tones.

steps.question: How do you say "I am not"?

options.label: 我不是 — wǒ bú shì
options.why: Correct, including the tone change on 不.

options.label: 我是不 — wǒ shì bù
options.why: Word order is wrong. 不 always goes BEFORE the verb it negates.

lessons.title: 很 — the word that is not "very"

steps.title: A rule that surprises everyone
steps.body: You cannot say "I good" in Chinese by putting 我 next to 好. Adjectives need a linking word, and that word is 很.

steps.note: Dictionaries say 'very', but most of the time it means nothing at all — it is just glue.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: I + 很 + good = "I'm fine". Note there is no 是 here. With adjectives you use 很, not 是. Mixing those up is a classic beginner error.

options.label: 我很好
options.why: Right. Adjectives take 很, never 是.

options.label: 我是好
options.why: No. 是 links two nouns. For adjectives you need 很.

steps.title: Watch the tones
steps.big: wǒ hěn hǎo → wó hén hǎo
steps.body: Three tone 3s in a row. The first two both shift up to tone 2. Say it out loud — it is much easier that way than it looks written down.

lessons.title: 谢谢 and 请 — thanks and please

steps.note: Remember: x is sh. This is "shyeh-shyeh". The second syllable is light and quick.
q is ch, so this is "ching". Put it in front of any verb to make it polite.

steps.title: The most useful phrase you will learn
steps.body: "Please say that again." When someone speaks too fast — which will be always, at first — this is the sentence that keeps the conversation alive instead of killing it.

steps.note: Literally 'don't be polite'. Note 不 flipped to bú again — 客 is tone 4.

steps.title: Let's see what stuck
steps.body: You have met eight words. These questions show pinyin only — read it aloud before you answer, using everything from unit A.

options.label: I, me
options.why: Correct.

options.label: you
options.why: That is nǐ 你.

options.label: good
options.why: That is hǎo 好.

options.label: hello
options.why: Correct — and remember it is said ní hǎo.

options.label: thank you
options.why: That is xièxie 谢谢.

options.label: I am
options.why: That is wǒ shì 我是.

options.label: I am not
options.why: Correct, including the tone change on bù → bú.

options.label: I am
options.why: The 不 makes it negative.

options.label: you are not
options.why: That would start with nǐ.

steps.question: How do you pronounce the first sound?

options.label: sh, as in sheep
options.why: Right — pinyin x is a light sh.

options.label: ks, as in box
options.why: No. x is never ks in pinyin.

steps.title: That is unit B started
steps.body: Eight words, and you can already form a sentence. Next unit turns them into real exchanges.

lessons.title: A character is a meaning, not a letter

steps.title: Why the characters look like nothing you know
steps.body: A Chinese character is not a letter and you cannot sound it out. Each one is a whole syllable AND a whole meaning at once. Pinyin tells you how to say it; the character tells you what it means. That is why every word you have met comes with both.

steps.title: One character, one syllable, one meaning
steps.body: This is said rén and it means person. Nothing inside it spells r-e-n. Think of it like the symbols on a road sign: you know what they mean without reading any letters.

steps.title: Some started as pictures
steps.body: The oldest characters were drawings, simplified over three thousand years. Only a few hundred work this way, but they are the foundation for everything else. Once you see the picture you will not forget it.

steps.note: Keep an eye on this one. It turns up inside a huge number of characters, usually ones about eating or speaking.
Once drawn as a circle with a dot in the middle. Brush writing turned it square.

options.label: mouth
options.why: Right — 口 kǒu, an open mouth. You will spot it inside many other characters.

options.label: sun
options.why: The sun is 日, which has a line across the middle. 口 is empty: an open mouth.

options.label: person
options.why: Person is 人, the two walking legs. 口 is a mouth.

options.label: big
options.why: Right — 大 dà: a person 人 stretching their arms out as wide as they go.

options.label: person
options.why: Close. 人 is a person; 大 is a person with arms spread wide, which means big.

options.label: small
options.why: Small is 小, three tiny specks. 大 is the wide one: big.

steps.title: The secret that makes characters learnable
steps.body: Most characters are not pictures. They are two or three smaller parts put together, and the parts carry hints: one usually points at the MEANING, another often at the SOUND. There are only about 200 common parts. Learn the parts and a new character stops being a random squiggle.

steps.note: So the 好 in 你好 literally contains a woman and a child. That is the whole word "good".

steps.title: Parts squeeze to fit
steps.body: When a part sits on the left of a character it gets squeezed thinner. Person 人 becomes 亻. It looks different but it means exactly the same thing.

steps.note: The left half says "this is about a person". The right half, 尔, is only there for the sound.

steps.question: All three have 亻 on the left. What does that tell you?

options.label: They are about people
options.why: Exactly. 你 you, 他 he, 们 the plural of people. 亻 marks the meaning.

options.label: They sound the same
options.why: No — nǐ, tā and men sound nothing alike. 亻 hints at the meaning (person), not the sound.

options.label: They are all verbs
options.why: No. 亻 means person, and these are all words for people: you, he, and a plural marker.

steps.title: Three parts that explain dozens of characters
steps.body: Some parts are so common that knowing them lets you guess what a character is about before you have ever seen it. These three are worth learning first.

steps.note: 谢谢 xièxie, thank you, is simply this character twice.
Anything you do with your mouth tends to carry 口: eating 吃, drinking 喝, and even the question word 吗.

steps.question: You have never seen this character. What is it probably about?

options.label: Language, speaking
options.why: Yes. 语 yǔ means language — 汉语 is "Chinese language". The 讠 on the left gave it away.

options.label: Food
options.why: Food characters usually carry 饣 or 口. The left part here is 讠, speech.

options.label: A feeling
options.why: Feelings carry 心 or 忄. The left part here is 讠, which means speech.

steps.question: Which part gives away what this character is about?

options.label: 口 on the left — something done with the mouth
options.why: Right. 喝 hē means to drink, and the 口 told you it is a mouth thing.

options.label: 讠 — something spoken
options.why: There is no 讠 here. The left part is 口, mouth: 喝 is to drink.

options.label: 亻 — a person
options.why: There is no 亻 here. The left part is 口, mouth: 喝 is to drink.

lessons.title: Reading the words you already say

steps.title: You have been saying these for days
steps.body: Here are the characters behind words you already know. Not every one breaks down neatly — a few you just learn as a shape, and that is normal.

steps.note: Its parts do not help much today. Learn this one as a shape: the little word that links 我 to 好 in 我很好.

options.label: I am
options.why: Right — 我 wǒ (I) + 是 shì (to be).

options.label: You are
options.why: You would be 你, with the person part 亻 on the left. 我 is I.

options.label: I am not
options.why: That needs 不 in the middle: 我不是.

options.label: Hello
options.why: Right — 你 you + 好 good. Literally "you good".

options.label: Thank you
options.why: Thank you is 谢谢, the speech character twice.

options.label: I am good
options.why: That would start with 我 (I): 我很好.

options.label: Thank you
options.why: Right — 谢 twice. The 讠 on the left marks it as something you say.

options.label: Please
options.why: Please is 请. It shares the 讠 speech part, but the right side is different.

options.label: To speak
options.why: To speak is 说. Same 讠 on the left — both are about speech — but a different character.

steps.title: Where the characters go from here
steps.body: Every new word on the path now shows what each of its characters means and what it is built from. The Script tab has all the characters in this course with a short daily practice, and the ones from these lessons are already in it. Characters stay optional: you can learn to speak without them.

lessons.title: 你好吗？— asking how someone is

steps.title: Turning any statement into a question
steps.body: Add 吗 to the end of a statement and it becomes a yes/no question. No word order changes, no rising intonation needed. 吗 is neutral tone — light and quick.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: 你好 (you good) + 吗 = "Are you good?" — how are you.

steps.title: And the answer
steps.body: "I'm fine, thanks." You now have a complete two-line exchange.

steps.question: How would you ask "Are you American?" given 你是美国人 = you are American?

options.label: 你是美国人吗？
options.why: Right — just add 吗 to the end. Nothing else moves.

options.label: 吗你是美国人？
options.why: 吗 always goes at the very end, never the start.

options.label: 你吗是美国人？
options.why: 吗 belongs at the end of the whole sentence.

steps.note: Mouth 口 on the left — it is something you say.

steps.title: Question words stay put
steps.body: "You are called what name?" In English the question word jumps to the front. In Chinese it stays exactly where the answer would go — which makes questions much easier than you expect.

steps.title: Answering
steps.body: Just put your name where 什么 was. 我叫 + your name. That is the whole answer.

steps.question: Where does 什么 (what) sit in a question?

options.label: Exactly where the answer would go
options.why: Right — this is one of the genuinely easy things about Chinese grammar.

options.label: At the front, like English
options.why: No. Chinese leaves the question word in place.

steps.title: The most valuable sentences you will learn
steps.body: Not greetings. These. When a conversation gets away from you, these three keep it going instead of ending it in an embarrassed silence.

steps.title: 1. I don't understand
steps.body: Literally "I listen-not-understand" — specifically about hearing, which is exactly your situation as a beginner.

steps.title: 2. Please say it again
steps.body: You met this in lesson 13. It is worth over-learning.

steps.title: 3. Please speak slower
steps.body: People genuinely will slow down. Almost nobody minds.

steps.title: You can now hold a short conversation
steps.body: Greet someone, exchange names, say how you are, and recover when you get lost. That is a real, usable set — and it is only lesson 17.

steps.title: A whole exchange
steps.body: Everything below uses only words you have met. Read each line aloud before checking.

steps.pinyin: nǐ hǎo! nǐ jiào shénme míngzi?
steps.question: What is being said?

options.label: Hello! What's your name?
options.why: Correct.

options.label: Hello! How are you?
options.why: That would be 你好吗 nǐ hǎo ma.

options.label: Thank you! I'm fine.
options.why: No 谢谢 or 很好 in that line.

steps.pinyin: wǒ jiào Lǐ Míng. nǐ ne?
steps.question: What is being said?

options.label: My name is Li Ming. And you?
options.why: Correct — 呢 ne bounces the question back.

options.label: I don't understand.
options.why: That is 我听不懂.

options.label: I am not Li Ming.
options.why: There is no 不 in that line.

options.label: Sorry, I don't understand
options.why: Correct.

options.label: Sorry, I'm late
options.why: 听不懂 is specifically about not understanding what you heard.

steps.prompt: Greet someone and ask their name
steps.pinyin: ní hǎo, nǐ jiào shénme míngzi

steps.title: That is the guided path, for now
steps.body: Eighteen lessons: you can read pinyin, hear all four tones, and hold a short exchange. From here the Review tab keeps these from fading, and Talk puts them into real conversations. More lessons are coming — this path is built to grow.
